p: The collection of rare coins ______ displayed in a locked glass case near the museum’s entrance.
x: The subject is “collection” (singular). “Of rare coins” is just a describing phrase.
t: “Coins” sits right before the blank and tempts you toward a plural verb.

p: Each of the students who entered the science fair ______ required to submit a written report.
x: “Each” is singular, so it takes “was.”
t: “Students” is inside the phrase “of the students,” so it isn’t the subject.

p: The results of the survey, which was conducted over three months, ______ that most residents support the new park.
x: The subject is “results” (plural). Skip the phrase and the clause between commas.
t: “Survey” is singular, but it isn’t the subject of this verb.

p: When the museum reopened after renovations, ______ new wing featured interactive exhibits about local history.
x: The museum (singular) owns the wing, so use the possessive “its.”
t: “It’s” means “it is.” Test it: “it is new wing” doesn’t work.

p: The two scientists published ______ findings in a leading journal last spring.
x: Plural owners (two scientists) take the plural possessive “their.”
t: “There” is a place, and “they’re” means “they are.”

p: Neither the coach nor the players ______ expecting the storm to delay the game.
x: With “neither … nor,” the verb agrees with the closer subject: “players” (plural), so “were.”
t: “Coach” comes first, but the closer noun decides.

p: The ______ reports, written by all twenty-five members of the class, were collected at the end of the semester.
x: Many students own the reports, so use the plural possessive: students’.
t: “Student’s” would mean one student, but the text says twenty-five members wrote them.

p: Walking through the ancient ruins, ______
c: the visitors noticed carvings that had survived for centuries.
carvings that had survived for centuries caught the visitors’ attention.
the carvings had survived for centuries, and the visitors noticed them.
centuries had passed, but the visitors still noticed the carvings.
x: Whoever is walking must come right after the comma. Only the visitors can walk.
t: In the second choice, the carvings would be walking, which is a dangling modifier.

p: By the time the rescue team arrived, the hikers ______ for nearly six hours.
x: The waiting happened before another past event (the team arrived), so use the past perfect: “had been waiting.”
t: Present-tense choices clash with “arrived.”

p: Every summer, the town ______ a festival that celebrates its founding, and thousands of visitors attend.
x: “Every summer” and “attend” are present tense, so the verb is “hosts.”
t: “Hosted” is past tense and clashes with “attend.”

p: The novel’s main character, a retired sailor who spends his days repairing old ______ is based on the author’s grandfather.
x: The extra description opened with a comma after “character,” so it must close with a comma.
t: A dash can’t close a phrase that a comma opened. Match the pair.

p: The architect ______ designed the city’s tallest building also created several of its public parks.
x: The blank is the subject of “designed,” and it refers to a person, so use “who.”
t: “Which” is for things, and “whom” is for objects.

p: The recipe calls for three main ______ flour, butter, and sugar.
x: A complete sentence followed by a list: a colon introduces it.
t: A semicolon needs complete sentences on both sides, and “flour, butter, and sugar” isn’t one.

p: Among the items found in the time capsule ______ a newspaper from 1925, a pocket watch, and a letter to future residents.
x: The sentence is inverted. The real subject comes after the verb: three items, so “were.”
t: “Time capsule” sits right before the blank, but it’s inside a phrase.

p: The flock of geese ______ south every autumn, stopping at the same lake along the way.
x: “Flock” is a singular collective noun, so it takes “flies.”
t: “Geese” is inside the phrase “of geese,” and “flying” would leave the sentence without a main verb.

p: The hikers took off ______ backpacks and sat down to rest at the summit.
x: The hikers (plural) own the backpacks, so use “their.”
t: “They’re” means “they are.”

p: The team’s goals are to make the software easier to use, to reduce its cost, and ______
x: Items in a list must be parallel: “to make … to reduce … to improve.”
t: “Improving” breaks the “to ___” pattern.

p: Each of the paintings in the exhibit has a small card beside ______ that explains the work’s history.
x: Each card sits beside one painting (“each”), so use the singular “it.”
t: “Them” agrees with “paintings,” but the subject is “each.”

p: The documentary, which features interviews with dozens of ______ explores how the city’s music scene changed over fifty years.
x: The extra clause opened with a comma after “documentary,” so it closes with a comma.
t: Leaving it out makes the reader think the musicians explore the music scene.

p: The documentary—which features interviews with dozens of ______ explores how the city’s music scene changed over fifty years.
x: The interruption opened with a dash, so it must close with a dash.
t: A comma can’t close a dash-opened phrase. Match the pair.

p: Once a small fishing village, the town ______ into a popular tourist destination over the past century.
x: “Over the past century” describes change up to now, so use the present perfect: “has grown.”
t: “Is growing” describes something happening right now, not over a whole past century.

p: Researchers studying the fossil ______ that the animal was about the size of a house cat.
x: The sentence needs a main verb for “Researchers.” Only “concluded” is one.
t: “Concluding” and “having concluded” can’t be main verbs, so they leave a fragment.

p: The city’s oldest ______ built in 1850, is now a museum dedicated to local history.
x: “Built in 1850” is extra information set off by a pair of commas, and the closing comma is already there.
t: Without the opening comma, the sentence has a lone comma between the subject and the verb.

p: The number of students enrolled in the robotics club ______ doubled since last year.
x: “The number” is singular. (“A number of” would be plural.)
t: “Students” and “robotics club” are both inside phrases.

p: Unlike ______ the new phone model has a battery that lasts two full days.
x: An introductory phrase is followed by a comma before the main sentence.
t: A semicolon or colon needs a complete sentence before it.

p: Of the twelve entries in the competition, the judges were most impressed by one ______ design, which used recycled materials to build a solar-powered shelter.
x: “One team” owns the design, so use the singular possessive: team’s.
t: “Teams’” is plural possessive, which clashes with “one.”

p: Known for its bright red feathers, ______
c: the northern cardinal is a common sight at backyard bird feeders.
backyard bird feeders often attract the northern cardinal.
many people enjoy seeing the northern cardinal at feeders.
bird watchers often spot the northern cardinal at feeders.
x: The thing known for red feathers must come right after the comma: the cardinal.
t: The other choices put feeders, people, or bird watchers right after the comma.

p: The orchestra performed three pieces: a symphony by Mozart, a concerto by Vivaldi, ______ a new work by a local composer.
x: The comma before the blank is already there, so just add “and” before the last item.
t: Don’t put a comma after “and.”

p: The scientist’s notebooks, ______ were donated to the university after her death, contain detailed sketches of the plants she studied.
x: After a comma, an extra (nonessential) clause about things uses “which.”
t: “They” would create a comma splice, and “that” can’t follow a comma in this kind of clause.

p: Last year, the school ______ a new policy that lets students use calculators on all math tests.
x: “Last year” calls for the past tense.
t: The other choices don’t match a finished past action.

p: The Sahara Desert, which covers much of North Africa, ______ roughly the same size as the United States.
x: The subject is “The Sahara Desert” (singular). Skip the clause between commas.
t: “Being” leaves the sentence without a main verb.
